title: Word meaning in context
blurb: Answer 'As used in paragraph 2, the word ___ most nearly means' items using context clues, the right sense of a multiple-meaning word and plain readings of figurative phrases.
question: A HESI A2 passage says a clinic now 'discharges patients through a side exit,' and the question asks: 'As used in paragraph 2, the word discharge most nearly means...' One option is 'release fluid from.' Why is that a trap, and how does the paragraph tell you the right meaning?

teach.body: Formally, a word's meaning in context is the sense the surrounding words, sentences and paragraph give it, which may differ from its most common meaning. Context clues are the hints that reveal that sense. On the HESI A2 the stem reads 'As used in paragraph 2, the word ___ most nearly means...' Plain English: the question is not 'Do you know this word?' but 'Can you read what this paragraph makes it mean?'

head: Clue type
Signal words
Example
rows: is, means, or, that is, in other words
because, since, so, as a result
the meaning of the whole paragraph
teach.caption: A phrase set off by commas or parentheses right after the word is usually a definition clue.

teach.h: Multiple-meaning words: common vs in context
teach.caption: When a familiar word sounds odd in its sentence, another of its meanings is in play.

teach.h: Figurative phrases (low weight on the HESI)
head: Device
How it works
Plain meaning
rows: 'felt like climbing a mountain' = very hard
'running on fumes' = nearly out of energy
'a thousand miles of hallway' = a lot

teach.body:
(1) After hip surgery, patients are encouraged to become ambulatory, or able to walk on their own, as soon as their surgeon allows. Unlike sedentary patients, who spend most of the day in a bed or chair, early walkers tend to regain strength faster.

(2) The first walk can feel like climbing a mountain. Nurses stay close, and a physical therapist checks that the patient's balance is steady before adding distance.

(3) Most patients are discharged within a few days. Before they leave, staff make sure each person can manage stairs, because a fall at home can undo weeks of progress.

teach.h: Scenario: Priya works four stems on the passage
items: 'As used in paragraph 1, ambulatory...': 'or' introduces a restatement. Meaning: able to walk on their own.
'As used in paragraph 1, sedentary...': 'Unlike' contrasts with early walkers, and the clause explains: in a bed or chair. Meaning: inactive.
'As used in paragraph 2, feel like climbing a mountain...': a simile. Plain meaning: very hard, not literally climbing.
'As used in paragraph 3, discharged...': patients leave after care, so the meaning is sent home, not the fluid sense Priya first thinks of from nursing.

teach.body: Before you look at the options, cover the word and put your own simple word in the gap. Then substitute each option into the sentence and reread the paragraph. The right answer keeps both the meaning and the tone. If an option makes the paragraph contradict itself ('Unlike Tasha, who chatted easily, Joel was talkative'), it is wrong, however familiar it sounds.

steps.label: Cover the word
steps.sub: do not guess from its look

head: Trap
What it looks like
rows: The word's everyday sense, not this paragraph's
Meaning of a similar word: eminent vs imminent
A synonym of a word next to the target
The trait of the person being contrasted
teach.caption: Trap answers are real meanings of real words. Substitution, not familiarity, decides.

teach.text: In health passages the most tempting wrong answer is often the word's medical sense: 'discharge' as fluid, 'acute' as a kind of illness, 'positive' as a test result. The paragraph decides. In a contrast clue the meaning is the opposite of the nearby description: in 'Unlike chatty Tasha, Joel was reticent', 'talkative' describes Tasha, not Joel.

items: Stem: 'As used in paragraph 2, the word ___ most nearly means': go to that paragraph and read around the word.
Six clue types: definition, synonym, contrast, example, cause and effect, general sense.
For a multiple-meaning word, pick the sense that fits this paragraph, not the most common one.
Translate figurative phrases (simile, metaphor, idiom, hyperbole) into their plain meaning.
Predict, then substitute: the key keeps meaning and tone; traps are common meanings, look-alikes, nearby words and contrast flips.

summary: You can now work out what a word or phrase means as used in a specific paragraph, using context clues and the substitution check. You can also choose the right sense of a multiple-meaning word and translate figurative phrases into plain meaning.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Many adults over 65 take five or more medicines every day, often prescribed by different doctors who may not know about one another's orders.

(2) Pharmacists call this pattern polypharmacy, that is, the regular use of several drugs at the same time. They watch for it closely, because each added medicine raises the chance that two drugs will interact in a harmful way.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "polypharmacy" most nearly means
options: the regular use of several drugs
a review of a patient's medicines
A.why: 'That is' signals a restatement: the paragraph defines the word as 'the regular use of several drugs at the same time'.

whyNot.0: Nearby-idea trap: a harmful interaction is the risk polypharmacy raises, not the pattern itself.
whyNot.2: A guess from the look of the word ('pharmacy'); the paragraph defines it after 'that is'.
whyNot.3: Pharmacists watch for polypharmacy; a review is their response, not the word's meaning.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The two new nursing assistants on the evening shift could hardly have been more different.

(2) Unlike Tasha, who chatted easily with every patient and visitor, Joel was reticent at first. He answered questions politely but seldom started a conversation, and he spent his breaks reading alone. By the end of the month, though, patients were asking for him by name.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "reticent" most nearly means
A.why: 'Unlike' contrasts Joel with chatty Tasha, and the next sentence says he seldom started a conversation: reticent means reserved.

whyNot.0: Contrast flip: talkative describes Tasha, the person Joel is contrasted with.
whyNot.1: Nothing questions Joel's skill; patients later ask for him by name.
whyNot.3: The paragraph says he answered questions politely.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Bright Street Clinic sees more than 200 patients on a typical Monday.

(2) To keep the waiting room from overflowing, staff now discharge patients through a side exit once their visit ends, so that people leaving do not cross paths with people checking in. The change has cut crowding at the front desk by nearly half.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "discharge" most nearly means
A.why: Patients leave through the side exit 'once their visit ends': staff send them out after their care. Substituting 'send out' keeps the meaning.

whyNot.0: Medical-sense trap: wound discharge is a real meaning, but nothing is released from the patients here.
whyNot.1: Common meaning in the workplace: the patients are not employees being fired.
whyNot.2: Other sense (discharged from service); the patients have no duty to be relieved of.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) For years, the county's only bridge to the hospital was a narrow two-lane span built in 1931.

(2) Because heavy trucks and decades of winter salt had left its steel supports badly rusted, inspectors judged the bridge precarious and closed it to all traffic until repairs were finished. Ambulances were rerouted along a road that added twelve minutes to each trip.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "precarious" most nearly means
B.why: Cause and effect: rusted supports (cause) led inspectors to close the bridge (effect). A bridge closed for that reason is unsafe.

whyNot.1: Nearby detail: the bridge was built in 1931, but the closing is explained by rust, not age alone.
whyNot.2: Heavy traffic is a cause of the wear, not what 'precarious' says about the bridge.
whyNot.3: Nearby-word trap: 'narrow' describes the bridge in paragraph 1, not the target word.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Most sore throats are caused by viruses and improve on their own within a week.

(2) The clinic's handout tells parents to call right away, however, if a child's sore throat comes with acute pain that makes swallowing almost impossible, or with a fever above 102°F. Those signs can point to an infection that needs a doctor's attention.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "acute" most nearly means
B.why: Pain that makes swallowing almost impossible, listed as a reason to call right away, is severe pain.

whyNot.0: Opposite: mild pain would not make swallowing almost impossible or need a call right away.
whyNot.2: This is closer to 'chronic', and nothing in the paragraph is about how long the pain lasts.
whyNot.3: Other sense: an acute angle in geometry; pain is not angled.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The Westfield family shelter opened in 1987 with twelve beds and one part-time nurse.

(2) Today its staff describe the shelter as resilient. Like the families it serves, it has weathered funding cuts, a flood and a fire, and each time it has bounced back and reopened within weeks.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "resilient" most nearly means
B.why: The synonym clue follows: it 'bounced back and reopened within weeks' after each setback. Resilient means quick to recover.

whyNot.0: Loose fit: a shelter may be generous, but the paragraph is about recovering from setbacks.
whyNot.1: Nearby detail: the 1987 opening is in paragraph 1 and says nothing about recovery.
whyNot.3: Opposite: the shelter has survived funding cuts.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Ana had worked double shifts at the diner all week while studying for her nursing entrance exam.

(2) By Friday she was, in her words, running on fumes. She fell asleep over her flash cards twice and told her sister she could not remember a single formula. On Saturday she slept for eleven hours and woke up ready to study again.

As used in paragraph 2, the phrase "running on fumes" most nearly means
C.why: An idiom: a car running on fumes has almost no fuel left. Ana falls asleep over her cards and then sleeps eleven hours: she was nearly out of energy.

whyNot.0: Literal reading of 'fumes'; the idiom is not about air.
whyNot.1: Cause, not meaning: the double shifts explain why she was exhausted.
whyNot.2: Near miss: nothing says her exam was close; the details describe tiredness.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Patients often hesitate to tell a provider how much they really drink, smoke or skip their medicines.

(2) Dr. Osei tries to make honesty easy. Rather than asking guarded yes-or-no questions, she invites patients to be candid, and she thanks them when they admit something difficult. Many tell her more than they have told any other doctor.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "candid" most nearly means
C.why: 'Tries to make honesty easy' and patients admitting difficult things show the meaning: candid means frank and honest.

whyNot.1: Loose fit from 'yes-or-no questions'; patients tell her more, not less.
whyNot.2: Contrast flip: 'guarded' describes the questions she avoids.
whyNot.3: Patients may be polite, but the paragraph is about honesty, not manners.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Before the city council voted on new bike lanes, it hired an outside firm to study traffic on the busiest streets.

(2) Council members praised the report as sound. Its counts covered every hour of the day for a full month, and two separate teams checked the figures. Even members who opposed the lanes said they trusted its numbers.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "sound" most nearly means
C.why: Complete counts, double-checked figures and trust even from opponents all show that the report was reliable.

whyNot.0: Common meaning (a noise); a report cannot be loud.
whyNot.2: Loose fit: a month of counts is long, but the praise is about trustworthy numbers.
whyNot.3: Opponents trusted the numbers, so the praise is for reliability, not for supporting one side.

reteach.title: Fill in the smudged word
reteach.question: A coffee spill has smudged one word on a note from your roommate: 'I'm ______ tonight, so please don't wake me before 6 a.m.' You know what the word must be without seeing it. That instinct is context-clue reading.

blocks.body: You filled the smudge with 'exhausted' or 'working late' because the rest of the note left only a few possibilities. An unfamiliar word in a HESI A2 passage is a smudge you can see: 'I'm somnolent tonight, so please don't wake me.' Treat it as blank, use the surrounding words to predict, and pick the option that fits the gap. The same works for a familiar word used in an unfamiliar sense: 'the report was sound' leaves room only for 'reliable'.

steps.label: Match an option
steps.sub: the one that fits the gap

blocks.text: Do not let a word's look or its most familiar meaning decide. 'Somnolent' looks like 'solemn', and 'sound' usually means noise, but substitution shows which sense fits the note or the paragraph.

explain.body: A definition clue states the meaning, often after 'or', 'that is', 'means' or between commas. A synonym clue places a word with a similar meaning nearby, often after 'also', 'likewise' or 'and'.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Hikers who climb high mountains too quickly can become ill from the thinner air.

(2) Rangers urge visitors to acclimatize, or let their bodies adjust gradually to the altitude, by spending a night at a middle elevation before climbing higher.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "acclimatize" most nearly means
test.why: 'Or' introduces the definition: 'let their bodies adjust gradually to the altitude'.

whyNot.0: Opposite: climbing too quickly is what makes hikers ill.
whyNot.1: Nearby-detail trap: a night at a middle elevation is the method, not the meaning.
whyNot.3: Loose fit with thin air; the definition says adjust, not breathe.

explain.body: A contrast clue sets the unknown word against its opposite, signaled by 'but', 'however', 'unlike', 'whereas' or 'instead'. Find the opposite, then flip it.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The hospital's first set of home-care instructions ran to six pages.

(2) Whereas that first version was verbose, the new sheet says the same things on a single page of short, plain sentences, and patients say they actually read it.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "verbose" most nearly means
test.why: 'Whereas' contrasts the first version with one that says the same things on one page in short sentences, so the first version used too many words.

whyNot.0: Contrast flip: brevity describes the new sheet.
whyNot.1: The contrast is about length, not accuracy: both versions 'say the same things'.
whyNot.2: Nothing says the first version was hard to find; the contrast is length.

explain.body: Many words have several meanings. The stem asks for the one that fits this paragraph, and the trap is usually the most common or most medical meaning. Substitute each option and keep the one that makes the whole paragraph make sense.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) During the month of Ramadan, many Muslim adults fast from dawn until sunset.

(2) Hospital dietitians work with patients who wish to observe the fast, planning meals and snack times around it whenever it is safe to do so.

As used in paragraph 2, the word "observe" most nearly means
test.why: Patients who plan their meals around the fast are keeping it: to observe a fast means to follow it.

whyNot.1: Most common meaning: watching does not fit a fast the patients themselves keep.
whyNot.2: Other sense (to notice something); patients are not noticing the fast but keeping it.
whyNot.3: Other sense (to observe that... = to comment); nothing is said aloud.

explain.body: A simile compares with 'like' or 'as', a metaphor compares directly, an idiom is a set phrase, and hyperbole exaggerates. Translate each into its plain meaning; never take it literally.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The first week of clinical rotations is famously demanding for new nursing students.

(2) "I must have walked a thousand miles of hallway," said Marcus after his first twelve-hour shift on the surgical unit. He added that he had never been so glad to sit down.

As used in paragraph 2, the phrase "walked a thousand miles of hallway" most nearly means that Marcus
test.why: Hyperbole: no one walks a thousand miles in a shift. The exaggeration, and his relief at sitting down, mean he walked a great deal.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests he was lost; the phrase stresses distance.
whyNot.2: He worked one shift on the surgical unit.
whyNot.3: The exaggeration is about distance, not speed.
